parts.text:
[Sound effects: The rhythmic clack of a mechanical keyboard, the low hum of computer cooling fans, the occasional rumble of thunder.]

I take a sip of cold, stale coffee, my eyes burning from the harsh glare of three monitors illuminating my cramped safehouse. On the center screen is the app itself: *Wayfinder*. It’s currently the number one download on the marketplace, marketed as a community-driven safety and navigation tool. "Never walk alone," its slogan boasts. 

It makes me sick. 

I’ve spent the last 48 hours tearing apart *Wayfinder's* source code. Erebus is brilliant, I’ll give the bastard that. The tracking script is buried so deep within the app's background refresh protocols that standard cybersecurity sweeps glide right over it. Millions of people are walking around with a live wire in their pockets, broadcasting their daily routines, their late-night stops, their vulnerabilities. 

[Sound effects: A lighter flicks, a sharp inhale.]

The Agency told me I was paranoid. They said my suspension after the mess in Seattle was supposed to be a time for reflection, a time to "get my head straight." But they don't understand ghosts like Erebus. They play by the rules; Erebus rewrites them. That’s why I had to go rogue. When you're hunting a monster that lives in the wires, a badge is just a bullseye.

My fingers dance across the keyboard, executing a custom packet-sniffer I designed specifically for this. If I can't break Erebus's encryption, I can at least follow the weight of the data. All these millions of location pings have to be stored somewhere. They have to be processed.

"Come on..." I mutter, watching lines of code cascade down the right monitor like green rain. "You're arrogant. Arrogant people always leave a backdoor."

[Sound effects: A sharp, high-pitched beep from the terminal. A red window pops up.]

Gotcha.

He masked the data stream through a dozen dummy servers in Eastern Europe, but the latency is too low. The ping response is almost immediate. He's not storing this data halfway across the world. He's keeping it close. 

I run a quick triangulation on the encrypted data clusters. The map on my left monitor zooms in on the cityscape, bypassing the glittering downtown high-rises and settling on the industrial district. The docks. Specifically, an abandoned server farm that supposedly went bankrupt five years ago.

"So that's your Mount Olympus, Erebus," I whisper.

I stand up, the leather of my chair creaking, and walk over to the metal table by the door. I grab my shoulder holster, checking the magazine of my sidearm before sliding it into place. I don't know what kind of physical security a paranoid hacker employs, but I'm not walking in blind. Not again. 

I throw on my trench coat, pulling the collar up. 

[Sound effects: Gun slide racking, heavy deadbolt unlocking. The sound of the rain outside grows significantly louder.]

Erebus thinks he's a god, watching the city from his digital throne, playing chess with people's lives. But tonight, he’s going to learn a hard lesson. 

Gods can be dragged down into the mud. 

[Sound effects: A heavy door slams shut, cutting off the hum of the computers, leaving only the sound of the pouring rain.]
